title: Direct Model APIs vs High-Level Abstractions
description: Compare direct provider SDKs with Microsoft.Extensions.AI and Semantic Kernel through a hands-on architectural exercise.

data.text: The Spectrum of AI Integration in .NET

When building AI-powered systems in .NET, architects face a foundational design choice: should you call provider-native client libraries directly (such as OpenAI .NET SDK or Azure.AI.OpenAI), program against lightweight abstractions (Microsoft.Extensions.AI), or adopt an orchestrator framework (Semantic Kernel)? Understanding the trade-offs allows you to select the right tool rather than blindly adopting a framework.

rows: Full access to provider features & raw wire protocol
Clean, lightweight standard abstractions for DI & middleware

Low to Medium (abstraction layer with plugin conventions)
Good (kernel services can be registered with mocks)
Low (just REST client with typed DTOs)
Medium to High (agents, planners, plugins, memory)

data.text: Using the provider's direct SDK gives you direct visibility into exact wire payloads, raw HTTP status codes, and provider-specific error headers (such as quota resets and token rates). This is invaluable when diagnosing low-level communication issues.

data.title: Practical Architecture Comparison Exercise
data.description: Evaluate maintainability, unit testing, and vendor independence across both implementations.
steps: 1. Write an xUnit unit test for AbstractedTicketClassifier by creating a Mock<IChatClient> returning a canned response. Notice zero network calls or credentials needed.
2. Try writing a unit test for DirectOpenAiTicketClassifier. Notice how complex it is to mock ClientResult<ChatCompletion> or AzureOpenAIClient.
3. Switch the underlying model provider in AbstractedTicketClassifier from Azure OpenAI to Ollama (local model) with a one-line change in Program.cs.
4. Add a telemetry logging wrapper to measure execution latency across all prompts without changing the classifier class.
data.expectedOutcome: You will recognize that direct provider SDKs are best kept behind an abstraction boundary, using Microsoft.Extensions.AI as the enterprise standard in .NET.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Direct provider SDKs expose raw capabilities and are essential for debugging wire protocols
Microsoft.Extensions.AI provides lightweight, testable abstractions that integrate with standard .NET dependency injection
Semantic Kernel builds atop these abstractions to provide higher-level multi-agent orchestration and plugin mechanisms
Decoupling business logic from vendor SDKs through IChatClient drastically improves unit testability and shields against API deprecations
Use direct SDKs only when investigating provider-specific issues or consuming preview features not yet supported by standard abstractions
data.takeaway: Embrace abstractions like Microsoft.Extensions.AI for enterprise maintainability and testability, while retaining the knowledge of underlying provider APIs to diagnose edge cases.
